The link is for you, not for a reader. Almost nobody else clicks it, so the goal is not discoverability — it is getting out of the way while staying findable by the one person who already knows it is there. That is the argument for a mark rather than a tool: an icon of a pencil explains itself to an audience that does not need explaining to.

All three sit in the real metadata row at real size, next to a real date. Hover each.

A. The soapstone. A scrawl left on the ground — the Souls message, and the only one of the three that means someone wrote here and you may too rather than here is a tool. It is handwriting, so it is the most mysterious and the least likely to be mistaken for a control. Its weakness is that at 14px a loose scrawl can read as a smudge rather than as a mark.

B. The rune. Cut, not written: four straight strokes, asymmetric, the kind of thing carved into a doorpost. It matches the theme's inscriptional type more exactly than anything else here and it holds its shape at any size, because straight strokes always do. It is also the most opaque — it means nothing until you are told, which on a link only you use is a cost of exactly zero.

C — The feather

C. The feather. A quill with the pen taken out of it — writing implied rather than depicted, which is the difference between mysterious and instructional. Reads instantly, sits comfortably in the metadata row, and is the safest of the three. It is also the least strange: a feather is a shape everyone has seen on a website before.
